name: Minoxidil + finasteride stack

lead: Fin+min combines minoxidil, which stimulates hair growth, with finasteride, which lowers DHT, the hormone behind male pattern hair loss. It is the base regimen in looksmaxxing hair-retention threads for keeping hair and improving density.

The chain is two mechanisms at once: finasteride blocks type II and III 5-alpha-reductase, lowering scalp and serum DHT and slowing follicle miniaturisation, while minoxidil, a vasodilator prodrug, appears to prolong follicle growth. Each drug is FDA-approved for hair loss and beat placebo in randomised trials, including a 2017 meta-analysis; trials of the combination itself are small.

paras: People use topical minoxidil daily and finasteride as a daily pill, as a long-term routine started as early as possible. Visible changes typically take months, and results hold only while treatment continues.

Finasteride is linked to reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, mood effects and, in 2025, EMA-confirmed suicidal thoughts; whether effects persist after stopping is disputed. Minoxidil can cause scalp irritation and, orally, fluid retention and heart effects. Benefits fade when treatment stops.

angle.text: Finasteride lowers DHT and minoxidil stimulates follicles, so hair loss slows and density can improve. Both drugs are approved for male pattern hair loss and backed by randomised trials, and the pair is the usual starting regimen in hair communities.

lead: The minoxidil plus finasteride stack, often abbreviated "fin+min" on forums, is the combined use of minoxidil, which stimulates hair growth, and finasteride, which lowers dihydrotestosterone (DHT), to treat or slow male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia). Both drugs are FDA-approved for this purpose individually, and the pairing is the baseline hair-loss regimen discussed in looksmaxxing communities.[1][2]

Finasteride was approved by the FDA at 1 mg for male pattern hair loss in 1997 as Propecia, and topical minoxidil in August 1988 as Rogaine.[3][4] A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials found treatments including 5% and 2% minoxidil and 1 mg finasteride were superior to placebo for hair outcomes.[2] The drugs act by different mechanisms, and small trials have compared combined topical lotions with minoxidil alone.[5][6]

Finasteride carries documented sexual, mood and other adverse effects that are contested in their persistence, and in 2025 the European Medicines Agency confirmed suicidal thoughts as a possible side effect.[4]

paras: Minoxidil was developed by Upjohn, which synthesised it in 1963 and introduced it for high blood pressure in 1971 after researchers noticed hair growth as a side effect. It is a prodrug converted to minoxidil sulfate in hair follicles and is thought to open potassium channels and affect follicle blood supply and growth signalling, though the full mechanism is not settled.[3] It remains a long-term treatment: Wikipedia says effects are reversible and stopping leads to loss of gains.[3]

Finasteride inhibits type II and III 5-alpha-reductase, lowering serum DHT by roughly 70 percent and scalp DHT by 65 to 70 percent. Wikipedia reports meta-analyses finding about 15 percent regrowth, with the drug mainly slowing further loss and working best at the crown.[4]

A 2017 meta-analysis of randomised trials in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology in androgenetic alopecia found 5% minoxidil, 2% minoxidil, 1 mg finasteride and low-level laser therapy each superior to placebo.[2] A 2022 review ranked oral dutasteride, finasteride 5 mg, oral minoxidil 5 mg, finasteride 1 mg and low-dose oral minoxidil in decreasing probable efficacy.[1] A 2024 systematic review of 141 studies concluded that many treatments promote hair growth and highlighted a multifaceted, individualised approach.[7]

Registered trials have compared combination products with single agents, including a completed phase 3 trial of combined minoxidil and finasteride lotion versus minoxidil lotion and a 2023 phase 2/3 trial of topical finasteride plus minoxidil.[6][8] An Indian dermatology study reported maintenance of hair density in patients who replaced oral finasteride with minoxidil fortified with finasteride.[5]

The 2022 review reports that oral finasteride is associated with sexual dysfunction and neuropsychiatric effects, while oral minoxidil causes hypertrichosis and cardiovascular symptoms in a dose-dependent way.[1] Topical minoxidil commonly causes scalp irritation and dryness.[3]

For finasteride, Wikipedia reports reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and lower semen volume as common effects, about 1.5 percent risk of gynecomastia, and reports of depression and suicidality. It describes post-finasteride syndrome, persistent symptoms after stopping, as disputed; a 2019 BMJ editorial called it ill defined, and a 2021 meta-analysis found associations with limited evidence quality. The FDA updated labelling in 2012 for persistent sexual effects.[4] Merck settled most of about 1,370 product-liability suits by 2018.[4]

On looksmax.org, users commonly describe fin+min as the default hair-retention approach; a poster who had taken finasteride for about three and a half months asked whether to add minoxidil, said they were saving for another procedure, and described hair loss as severely distressing. Another reply in the same thread said finasteride causes permanent testicular shrinkage and lower testosterone, whereas Wikipedia describes the persistence of such effects as disputed.[4]

Evidence is split between trials of each drug alone and a few small trials of combined topical products. The 2017 meta-analysis covers single agents versus placebo.[2] Registered combination trials include NCT01391156 (completed, 40 participants) and NCT05990400 (40 participants).[6][8] Trials comparing the oral drugs together with each other in men are not described in these sources.

lore.intro: Fin+min is discussed on looksmax.org as the basic treatment against hair loss, with arguments over adding oral minoxidil, dutasteride, or avoiding finasteride because of side-effect fears.
